upgrade.title: Still saying “very good”?
upgrade.subtitle: Use stronger words in Speaking and Writing
upgrade.caption: 📌 Rule: use one strong adjective, not “very + a basic adjective”. Don't put “very” before strong adjectives: ❌ very exhausted → ✅ absolutely exhausted. 🗣 Example: I was exhausted after the exam, but delighted with my score.

upgrade.title: 1 verb in place of a phrasal verb
upgrade.subtitle: It sounds more formal in Writing Task 2
upgrade.caption: 📌 In Speaking, phrasal verbs are natural and good. But in Writing Task 2, one formal verb sounds stronger. ✍️ Example: Governments should consider ways to improve public transport.

upgrade.title: Giving your opinion in Speaking
upgrade.subtitle: Don't say “I think” in every sentence
upgrade.caption: 📌 “I think” is not wrong, but if you repeat it in every answer, your Lexical Resource score goes down. Use a different phrase each time. 🗣 Example: Do you like reading? — Oh, I'm really into it, especially detective novels.

upgrade.title: Change your linking words
upgrade.subtitle: For your Coherence & Cohesion score
upgrade.caption: 📌 Be careful: however usually comes at the start of a new sentence, with a comma after it. ❌ I like it, however it is expensive. ✅ I like it. However, it is expensive.

upgrade.title: Task 1: describing a graph
upgrade.subtitle: For line graphs and tables
upgrade.caption: 📌 Add an adverb to the verb and your description is clearer: increased steadily (went up at the same speed), dropped slightly (went down a little). ✍️ Example: Sales peaked at 80% in 2015 and then declined gradually.

upgrade.title: Forget “a lot of”
upgrade.subtitle: Talk about amounts in a clearer, more formal way
upgrade.caption: 📌 Note: a number of + things you can count (students), an amount of + things you can't count (money). ✍️ Example: A significant proportion of young people work part-time.

upgrade.title: Say goodbye to “good” and “bad”
upgrade.subtitle: Use more exact adjectives in your essay
upgrade.caption: 📌 These adjectives often come with a preposition: beneficial to, detrimental to. ✍️ Example: Excessive screen time is detrimental to children's eyesight.

upgrade.title: Speaking Part 1: after “Yes”
upgrade.subtitle: Start in a natural way, not with a short answer
upgrade.caption: 📌 In Part 1, don't stop after “Yes” or “No”. After the opening phrase, add 1–2 more sentences. 🗣 Example: Do you cook often? — More often than not, yes. I usually make dinner for my family.

upgrade.title: Say your feelings clearly
upgrade.subtitle: One strong word, not “very sad”
upgrade.caption: 📌 You will need these words for “Describe a time when…” questions in Speaking Part 2. 🗣 Example: I was absolutely terrified before my first exam, but astonished by my result.

upgrade.title: Describe a person
upgrade.subtitle: For “Describe a person” questions
upgrade.caption: 📌 One adjective is not enough: prove it with an example. 🗣 Example: My teacher is really approachable. You can ask her anything, even after class.

upgrade.title: Describe a place
upgrade.subtitle: When you talk about a city, a park or a café
upgrade.caption: 📌 bustling is positive (busy and full of life). crowded is often negative. 🗣 Example: The old town is bustling during the day but surprisingly tranquil at night.

upgrade.title: Make simple verbs stronger
upgrade.subtitle: Formal options for Writing Task 2
upgrade.caption: 📌 In Speaking, “get” and “buy” are natural. Formal verbs fit Writing better. ✍️ Example: Social media can exacerbate loneliness rather than enhance friendships.

upgrade.title: Topic: Education
upgrade.subtitle: For essays about education
upgrade.caption: 📌 Education is one of the most common topics in IELTS Writing Task 2. ✍️ Example: Regular assessment helps educators identify students who might drop out.

upgrade.title: Topic: Environment
upgrade.subtitle: For essays about the environment
upgrade.caption: 📌 These words often come in pairs with a verb: tackle air pollution, combat deforestation. ✍️ Example: Governments must take urgent action to combat deforestation.

upgrade.title: Topic: Technology
upgrade.subtitle: When you talk about technology
upgrade.caption: 📌 hooked is informal and good for Speaking. In Writing, say addicted to or dependent on. 🗣 Example: Smartphones have become indispensable, and many teenagers are hooked.

upgrade.title: Topic: Health
upgrade.subtitle: For questions about health
upgrade.caption: 📌 “fat” sounds rude when you talk about a person. In IELTS, always say overweight. ✍️ Example: People who have a poor diet are more likely to put on weight.

upgrade.title: Topic: Work
upgrade.subtitle: When you talk about jobs
upgrade.caption: 📌 be made redundant = to lose your job because the company needs fewer workers. “fired” is when it is your fault. 🗣 Example: My father has a high-pressure job and often puts in long hours.

upgrade.title: Time phrases
upgrade.subtitle: For Writing and Task 1
upgrade.caption: 📌 In Task 1, time phrases show the trend clearly. ✍️ Example: Sales grew rapidly and eventually doubled, while costs rose annually.

upgrade.title: Cause and result
upgrade.subtitle: To link ideas in your essay
upgrade.caption: 📌 After leads to and contributes to, use a noun or -ing: leads to pollution, contributes to improving. ✍️ Example: Urbanisation leads to congestion, which contributes to air pollution.

upgrade.title: Comparing phrases
upgrade.subtitle: For Task 1 and Task 2
upgrade.caption: 📌 whereas joins two opposite facts in one sentence. ✍️ Example: Men preferred football, whereas women's figures were comparable across all sports.

upgrade.title: Thinking phrases for Speaking
upgrade.subtitle: Say these, don't stay silent
upgrade.caption: 📌 These phrases give you 2–3 seconds to think and save your Fluency score. 🗣 Example: Hmm, that's a tricky one. I'd say it depends on the person's age.

upgrade.title: Topic: City
upgrade.subtitle: When you talk about city life
upgrade.caption: 📌 affordable housing is a very common pair in essays. ✍️ Example: Many residents of the metropolis struggle to find affordable housing.

upgrade.title: Talking about money
upgrade.subtitle: For Speaking and Writing
upgrade.caption: 📌 splash out on is informal and sounds great in Speaking. In Writing, say spend heavily on. 🗣 Example: I rarely splash out, but I bought exorbitant concert tickets last year.

upgrade.title: Topic: Travel
upgrade.subtitle: For questions about travel
upgrade.caption: 📌 You can't count accommodation: “accommodations” ❌. The spelling is often wrong too: two c's and two m's. 🗣 Example: We went sightseeing all day and the scenery was stunning.

upgrade.title: Sport and hobbies
upgrade.subtitle: When you talk about free time
upgrade.caption: 📌 take up = start a new activity, give up = stop doing it. 🗣 Example: I took up swimming last year, and now I work out three times a week.

upgrade.title: Essay conclusion
upgrade.subtitle: For the conclusion paragraph
upgrade.caption: 📌 Don't add a new idea in the conclusion: just repeat your position in different words. ✍️ Example: Having considered both sides, I believe it is essential that governments act now.

upgrade.title: Topic: Family
upgrade.subtitle: Band 7+ words about family
upgrade.caption: 📌 Use take after only when you are like a parent or an older relative. 🗣 Example: I take after my father; we share a close bond.

upgrade.title: Topic: Food
upgrade.subtitle: Talk about food in a natural way
upgrade.caption: 📌 Don't put “very” before starving and mouth-watering. They are already strong. 🗣 Example: Nothing beats my mum's home-cooked meals.

upgrade.title: Topic: Shopping
upgrade.subtitle: More exact words about shopping
upgrade.caption: 📌 splurge on = to spend a lot of money on one thing. 🗣 Example: I rarely splurge on designer labels; I'd rather find a bargain.

upgrade.title: Topic: Media
upgrade.subtitle: About the news and the media
upgrade.caption: 📌 You can't count misinformation: we don't say “a misinformation”. ✍️ Example: Social media accelerates the spread of misinformation.

upgrade.title: Topic: Crime
upgrade.subtitle: Writing words about crime
upgrade.caption: 📌 deter = to stop people from doing something by making them afraid. The most useful verb in crime essays. ✍️ Example: Harsh penalties may not deter young offenders.

upgrade.title: Topic: Government
upgrade.subtitle: About the government and the law
upgrade.caption: 📌 allocate funds to + an area: allocate funds to healthcare. ✍️ Example: The authorities should allocate more funds to public transport.

upgrade.title: Topic: Culture
upgrade.subtitle: Exact words about culture
upgrade.caption: 📌 heritage = the traditions and values that pass from parents to children over many years. ✍️ Example: Tourism can help preserve a nation's cultural heritage.

upgrade.title: Art and music
upgrade.subtitle: Talking about art
upgrade.caption: 📌 have something on repeat = to listen to one song again and again. Great for Speaking Part 1. 🗣 Example: Lately I've had this song on repeat.

upgrade.title: Books and films
upgrade.subtitle: For Speaking Part 2
upgrade.caption: 📌 gripping = so interesting that you can't stop reading. 🗣 Example: The plot was so gripping that I finished it in one night.

upgrade.title: Topic: Transport
upgrade.subtitle: About roads and transport
upgrade.caption: 📌 commute is a verb and a noun: my daily commute. ✍️ Example: Investing in public transport reduces congestion at peak hours.

upgrade.title: Topic: Housing
upgrade.subtitle: About homes
upgrade.caption: 📌 You can't count rent: not “a rent” but “the rent”. ✍️ Example: Rising property prices force young people to rent.

upgrade.title: Topic: Weather
upgrade.subtitle: Talk about the weather in a natural way
upgrade.caption: 📌 Don't put “very” before scorching and freezing. You can say “absolutely”. 🗣 Example: Summers in Tashkent are absolutely scorching.

upgrade.title: Topic: Science
upgrade.subtitle: About science and research
upgrade.caption: 📌 You can't count research: not “researches”. You can say “studies”. ✍️ Example: Research shows that cutting-edge technology improves diagnosis.

upgrade.title: Topic: Animals
upgrade.subtitle: About animals
upgrade.caption: 📌 You can't count wildlife, so it has no plural form. ✍️ Example: Deforestation destroys the habitat of many endangered species.

upgrade.title: Globalisation
upgrade.subtitle: About the global world
upgrade.caption: 📌 In Writing, use worldwide or across the globe in place of “all over the world”. ✍️ Example: Globalisation may homogenise cultures worldwide.

upgrade.title: Topic: Advertising
upgrade.subtitle: Task 2 about advertising
upgrade.caption: 📌 mislead = to make someone believe something that is not true. As an adjective: misleading advertising. ✍️ Example: Some adverts deliberately mislead consumers.

upgrade.title: Topic: Tourism
upgrade.subtitle: About tourism
upgrade.caption: 📌 overtourism = too many tourists in one place. A modern essay topic. ✍️ Example: Overtourism can harm the lives of locals.

upgrade.title: Topic: Energy
upgrade.subtitle: About energy
upgrade.caption: 📌 fossil fuels is always used in the plural. ✍️ Example: Fossil fuels will eventually be depleted.

upgrade.title: Social media
upgrade.subtitle: About social networks
upgrade.caption: 📌 go viral = to spread very fast and become popular. 🗣 Example: One of my videos went viral last year.

upgrade.title: Topic: Friendship
upgrade.subtitle: About friends
upgrade.caption: 📌 hit it off = to like each other from the first meeting. 🗣 Example: We hit it off immediately and became lifelong friends.

upgrade.title: Topic: Childhood
upgrade.subtitle: Talking about when you were a child
upgrade.caption: 📌 For past habits, use used to or would. 🗣 Example: I vividly recall how I used to play outside all day.

upgrade.title: Topic: Old age
upgrade.subtitle: Task 2 about older people
upgrade.caption: 📌 In formal writing, say the elderly or senior citizens, not “old people”. ✍️ Example: As life expectancy rises, more care for the elderly is needed.

upgrade.title: Topic: Success
upgrade.subtitle: About success
upgrade.caption: 📌 Pairs with achieve: achieve a goal / success / ambition. We don't say “make a goal”. 🗣 Example: If you persevere, you'll achieve your goal.

upgrade.title: Topic: Leadership
upgrade.subtitle: Talking about a leader
upgrade.caption: 📌 delegate = to give parts of your work to other people. 🗣 Example: A good manager knows how to delegate tasks.

upgrade.title: Task 1: percentages
upgrade.subtitle: Numbers in words
upgrade.caption: 📌 To avoid repeating the same number, change the percentage into words. ✍️ Example: A quarter of students walked to school, while the majority took the bus.

upgrade.title: Task 1: “about” numbers
upgrade.subtitle: When the number is not exact
upgrade.caption: 📌 If you can't see the exact number on the graph, use approximately or roughly. ✍️ Example: Sales reached just over 3 million in 2010.

upgrade.title: Task 1: process verbs
upgrade.subtitle: For a process diagram
upgrade.caption: 📌 In a process diagram we mostly use the passive voice. ✍️ Example: The beans are roasted and then ground into powder.

upgrade.title: Task 1: map verbs
upgrade.subtitle: Changes on a map
upgrade.caption: 📌 In a map task, write the changes in the passive with the present perfect / past simple. ✍️ Example: The factory was demolished and converted into a park.

upgrade.title: Adverbs of degree
upgrade.subtitle: In place of “very”
upgrade.caption: 📌 considerably / significantly + a comparative adjective: considerably cheaper. ✍️ Example: Prices are considerably higher than a decade ago.

upgrade.title: Adverbs of frequency
upgrade.subtitle: How often?
upgrade.caption: 📌 hardly ever = almost never. Don't use it with “not” in the same sentence. 🗣 Example: I hardly ever watch TV; I read on a daily basis.

upgrade.title: Phrases for emphasis
upgrade.subtitle: Make your idea stronger
upgrade.caption: 📌 needless to say comes at the start of the sentence, with a comma. ✍️ Example: Needless to say, education is particularly important.

upgrade.title: Problem words
upgrade.subtitle: Replace “problem”
upgrade.caption: 📌 exacerbate = to make a problem worse. A Band 8 verb. ✍️ Example: Urban sprawl exacerbates traffic issues.

upgrade.title: Solution words
upgrade.subtitle: Giving a solution
upgrade.caption: 📌 tackle / address + a problem: tackle unemployment. ✍️ Example: Governments must tackle pollution and curb emissions.

upgrade.title: Advantages and disadvantages
upgrade.subtitle: For an advantage essay
upgrade.caption: 📌 outweigh = to be bigger or more important: the benefits outweigh the drawbacks. ✍️ Example: In my view, the benefits clearly outweigh the downsides.

upgrade.title: Speaking Part 2: a story
upgrade.subtitle: Tell the event in a lively way
upgrade.caption: 📌 be over the moon = to be very happy. Use it for feelings in Part 2. 🗣 Example: All of a sudden, my name was called and I was over the moon.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: Slang lowers your score, so use the formal option
slang.caption: 📌 The examiner sees slang as the wrong style, and your Lexical Resource score goes down. ❌ The movie was mid, no cap. ✅ Honestly, the film was rather mediocre.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: Short forms are for chats, not for the exam
slang.caption: 📌 In Speaking you can say “gonna”, but in Writing you must write the full form. ❌ I'm gonna explain why… ✅ I am going to explain why…

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: When you talk about places and food
slang.caption: 📌 Very useful in Speaking Part 2 when you describe a café, a restaurant or a place. ❌ The food was bussin' and the vibe was great. ✅ The food was delicious and the atmosphere was cosy.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: When you describe people
slang.caption: 📌 Ready words for the question “Describe a person you admire”. ✅ My close friend has incredible charisma. She's a real role model for me.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: About success and failure
slang.caption: 📌 Use these for the topic “Describe an achievement”. ❌ I took an L in my first test. ✅ I faced a setback in my first test, but later I excelled.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: When you talk about feelings
slang.caption: 📌 You need feeling words a lot in Speaking Part 1 and 2. ❌ The trip was lit but kinda cringe. ✅ The trip was thrilling, though slightly embarrassing at times.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: When you give your opinion
slang.caption: 📌 You say “fr fr” to a friend, but “honestly” to the examiner. It is all about style. ✅ Honestly, in my view, this trend is quite concerning.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: Turn internet language into academic language
slang.caption: 📌 Useful for essays about technology and social media. ✅ Young people should spend more time outdoors instead of endless scrolling.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: In everyday conversation
slang.caption: 📌 Speaking Part 1 is about daily life, so these words can come out before you notice. ❌ I'm obsessed with coffee, for real. ✅ I'm really keen on coffee. I can't start my day without it.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: On the topic of social media
slang.caption: 📌 Social media is a favourite topic of Writing Task 2. Learn to turn internet words into academic language. ✅ Many influencers chase popularity by showing off expensive lifestyles.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: When you talk about studying
slang.caption: 📌 Ready phrases for the question “Describe a time you studied hard”. ❌ I crammed all night and aced it. ✅ I revised intensively the night before and did extremely well.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: When you give your opinion
slang.caption: 📌 “awesome” and “cool” are not wrong, but if you repeat them in every sentence, your vocabulary looks small. ✅ The view was truly impressive, though the service was appalling.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: On the topic of shopping
slang.caption: 📌 For the question “Describe something you bought recently”. ❌ My new fit was a steal. ✅ My new outfit was a real bargain, only half the usual price.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: About sport and hobbies
slang.caption: 📌 For “hobbies” questions in Speaking Part 1. ❌ Gym is a vibe, I'm hooked. ✅ I'm passionate about fitness; it's genuinely relaxing.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: When you talk about music
slang.caption: 📌 For the question “What kind of music do you like?” ✅ I'm into mainstream music, mostly catchy, upbeat songs.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: When you talk about money
slang.caption: 📌 In Writing, don't write “bucks”. Write the full name of the currency. ✅ Students are often short of money, so they avoid overpriced cafés.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: When you talk about work
slang.caption: 📌 For the Work topic. ✅ Many young people take a part-time job or choose to work remotely.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: About technology
slang.caption: 📌 In formal speech, don't shorten the names of apps. ✅ Young people are more tech-savvy, but they spend hours online.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: About travel
slang.caption: 📌 For the Travel topic. ✅ Visiting Japan is on my list of dreams, but I'd avoid overcrowded resorts.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: About family
slang.caption: 📌 In Speaking, use the full word, not the short form. ✅ I live with my family; my brother and I are very close.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: About the weather
slang.caption: 📌 For the question “What's the weather like in your country?” ✅ Summers are extremely hot, while winters can be bitterly cold.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: About study habits
slang.caption: 📌 For Part 3 questions on the Education topic. ✅ Before exams I focus completely, but sometimes I have poor concentration.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: About your city
slang.caption: 📌 For the question “Describe your hometown”. ✅ The city centre is always crowded, but my neighbourhood is peaceful.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: About your mood
slang.caption: 📌 To describe feelings in Part 2. ✅ I was excited at first, but later quite disappointed.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: About food
slang.caption: 📌 For Part 1 questions on the Food topic. ✅ I'm a real food lover; on busy days I just have a quick meal.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: About fashion
slang.caption: 📌 For the Fashion topic. ✅ I often buy second-hand clothes; it's cheaper and more sustainable.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: About films and series
slang.caption: 📌 For “Describe a film you enjoyed”. ✅ It's highly recommended; there's an unexpected turn at the end.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: About communication
slang.caption: 📌 For the Communication topic. ✅ We rarely meet, so we send each other messages instead.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: About success
slang.caption: 📌 When you talk about your achievements. ✅ I performed excellently in the final and improved a lot overall.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: About the environment
slang.caption: 📌 For Environment essays. ✅ More people try to live sustainably and protect nature.

slang.title: Don't make this mistake in the exam!
slang.subtitle: Agreeing and disagreeing
slang.caption: 📌 For discussion in Part 3. ✅ I completely agree it matters, but that's unlikely to change soon.

emoji.explanation: brainstorm = to collect ideas. Brainstorm for 3–5 minutes before Writing Task 2!
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: this is exactly what you should do before you start Writing Task 2.

emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: people say this when an exam was very easy 😉

emoji.explanation: break the ice = to make people feel relaxed when they first meet. “A joke helped break the ice.”
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: starting a conversation with people you don't know.

emoji.explanation: the elephant in the room = a problem everyone knows about but nobody talks about.
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: a big problem that everyone sees but nobody mentions.

options: kill two birds with one stone

emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: one action, two results.

emoji.explanation: recharge my batteries = to rest and get your energy back. Great for “weekend” questions in Speaking Part 1!
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: a great answer to “What do you do at weekends?” in Speaking Part 1.

emoji.explanation: carbon footprint = the amount of CO₂ a person puts into the air. For Environment essays.
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: one of the most popular phrases in Environment essays.

emoji.explanation: global warming = the Earth getting hotter. Synonym: climate change. Use the two of them in Writing.
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: our planet gets hotter every year…

emoji.explanation: raining cats and dogs = raining very hard. A funny phrase, but people use it less now.
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: a funny phrase for very bad weather.

emoji.explanation: an early bird = a person who gets up early. “I'm an early bird, so I study best in the morning.”
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: an answer to “Are you a morning person?” in Speaking Part 1.

emoji.explanation: a night owl = a person who stays up late at night. The opposite of an early bird.
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: the opposite of last week's riddle 😉

emoji.explanation: time is money = time is as valuable as money, so don't waste it.
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: a famous saying about the value of time.

emoji.explanation: burnout = being extremely tired after working too much. A useful word for Work and Education essays.
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: working too much until you have no energy left.

emoji.explanation: a couch potato = a lazy person who watches TV on the sofa all day.
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: a person who never gets up from the sofa.

emoji.explanation: the apple of my eye = the person I love the most. “My little sister is the apple of my eye.”
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: you say it about someone you love very much.

emoji.explanation: the tip of the iceberg = only the small part of a problem that you can see. Very useful in essays.
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: when you can see only a small part of the problem.

options: like a fish out of water
emoji.explanation: like a fish out of water = feeling uncomfortable in a new place. “On my first day abroad I felt like a fish out of water.”
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: when you feel uncomfortable in a place you don't know.

emoji.explanation: the key to success = the most important thing you need to succeed. “Consistency is the key to success.”
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: for the question “What makes people successful?” in Speaking Part 3.

emoji.explanation: money doesn't grow on trees = money is not easy to get.
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: something parents often say to their children 😄

emoji.explanation: see eye to eye = to agree with someone. “My brother and I don't always see eye to eye.”
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: having the same opinion as someone.

emoji.explanation: a global village = the world brought closer together by the internet. For Globalisation essays.
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: a favourite phrase in essays about globalisation.

emoji.explanation: brain drain = when skilled workers leave their country to work abroad. A great term for essays.
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: when smart specialists move to another country.

emoji.explanation: solar power = energy from the sun. Synonyms: solar energy, renewable energy.
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: for Energy and Environment essays.

emoji.explanation: remote work = working away from the office. Synonym: working from home.
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: a way of working that became very popular after the pandemic.

emoji.explanation: smartphone addiction = not being able to stop using your phone. Common in Technology essays.
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: you can't put your phone down.

emoji.explanation: tuition fees = the money you pay to study. A “scholarship” is money that is given to you to study.
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: the money you pay to a university.

emoji.explanation: once in a blue moon = very rarely. “I eat fast food once in a blue moon.”
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: about something that happens very rarely.

emoji.explanation: hit the books = to start studying hard. “Before the exam I really hit the books.”
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: what do you do before an exam?

options: let the cat out of the bag
emoji.explanation: let the cat out of the bag = to tell a secret by mistake.
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: an idiom about a secret.

emoji.explanation: under the weather = a little ill. “I'm feeling a bit under the weather today.”
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: when you don't feel well.

emoji.explanation: on cloud nine = extremely happy. For “happy moment” questions in Part 2.
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: how you feel on the day you get Band 8 in IELTS.

emoji.explanation: a blessing in disguise = something that looks bad at first but turns out to be good.
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: it looked bad, but it was really a good thing.

emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: finishing the working day.

emoji.explanation: time flies = time passes very fast. “Time flies when you're having fun.”
emoji.caption: 💡 Hint: something that flies as fast as a bird.

truefalse.sentence: I am agree with this opinion.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. “agree” is a verb, so we don't put “am” before it. Correct: “I agree with this opinion.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: is agree a verb or an adjective?

truefalse.sentence: He gave me some useful advices.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. You can't count “advice”, so it has no -s. Correct: “some useful advice” or “a piece of advice”.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: can you count advice?

truefalse.sentence: It depends on the situation.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct! “depend” always goes with “on”. “It depends of” is wrong.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which preposition goes with depend?

truefalse.sentence: She explained me the rule.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. explain something TO someone. Correct: “She explained the rule to me.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: what is the word order after explain?

truefalse.sentence: I have been to London last year.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. With a finished past time (last year) we use the Past Simple: “I went to London last year.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which tense does last year need?

truefalse.sentence: The number of students has increased.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct! “The number of” + singular verb (has). But “A number of students have…”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: does the number of take a singular or a plural verb?

truefalse.sentence: People is becoming more health-conscious.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. “people” is plural. Correct: “People are becoming more health-conscious.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: is people singular or plural?

truefalse.sentence: I look forward to hear from you.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. look forward to + -ing. Correct: “I look forward to hearing from you.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which verb form comes after look forward to?

truefalse.sentence: I'm interesting in music.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. “interesting” describes a thing, “interested” describes how you feel. Correct: “I'm interested in music.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: what is the difference between interesting and interested?

truefalse.sentence: She is good at cooking.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct! good AT + noun or -ing. “good in cooking” is wrong.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which preposition comes after good?

truefalse.sentence: I have 20 years old.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. We use “be” for age: “I am 20 years old” or just “I'm 20.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which verb do we use for age in English?

truefalse.sentence: Can you borrow me your pen?
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. lend = to give for a short time, borrow = to take for a short time. Correct: “Can you lend me your pen?”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: the difference between borrow and lend.

truefalse.sentence: Everyone has their own opinion.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct! “everyone” takes a singular verb (has), but “their” is fine and natural.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: is everyone singular or plural?

truefalse.sentence: He suggested me to apply.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. Correct: “He suggested that I apply” or “He suggested applying.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which structure comes after suggest?

truefalse.sentence: I live in Tashkent since 2015.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. With “since” we need the Present Perfect: “I have lived in Tashkent since 2015.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which tense does since 2015 need?

truefalse.sentence: The informations are useful.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. You can't count “information”: “The information is useful.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: can you count information?

truefalse.sentence: I am used to waking up early.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct! be used to + -ing = something is normal for you now.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which verb form comes after be used to?

truefalse.sentence: It's more better than before.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. “better” is already a comparative, so “more” is not needed. Correct: “much better”.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: what form is better already?

truefalse.sentence: We discussed about the problem.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. “discuss” takes no preposition: “We discussed the problem.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: do you need a preposition after discuss?

truefalse.sentence: If I would have time, I would go.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. We don't use “would” in the “if” part: “If I had time, I would go.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which tense goes in the if part of the sentence?

truefalse.sentence: Neither of the answers is correct.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct! “Neither of” + singular verb (is) is the formal and correct form.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: does neither of take a singular verb?

truefalse.sentence: My hobby is reading books.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct! But in Speaking, “I'm really into reading” sounds even more natural.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: can an -ing form come after hobby is?

truefalse.sentence: I didn't went to school yesterday.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. After “didn't” we use the base form of the verb: “I didn't go to school yesterday.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which verb form comes after didn't?

truefalse.sentence: There is many reasons for this.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. “reasons” is plural: “There are many reasons for this.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: is reasons singular or plural?

truefalse.sentence: She married with a doctor.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. “marry” takes no preposition: “She married a doctor.” Or: “She got married to a doctor.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: do you need a preposition after marry?

truefalse.sentence: Although it was raining, but we went out.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. “although” and “but” don't go together in one sentence: “Although it was raining, we went out.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: can although and but be in one sentence together?

truefalse.sentence: I have visited Samarkand three times.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct. A life experience with no time given, so we use the present perfect.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which tense do we use for an experience with no time?

truefalse.sentence: She don't like coffee.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. With she/he/it we use “doesn't”. Correct: “She doesn't like coffee.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which helping verb goes with “she”?

truefalse.sentence: The news are very surprising.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. You can't count “news”, and it is singular: “The news is very surprising.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: is news singular or plural?

truefalse.sentence: I'm looking forward to meeting you.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct. look forward to + -ing: looking forward to meeting.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which verb form comes after to here?

truefalse.sentence: He is more taller than his brother.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. “taller” is already a comparative. Correct: “He is taller than his brother.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: can you make a comparative adjective stronger twice?

truefalse.sentence: Despite of the rain, we went out.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. There is no “of” after “despite”. Correct: “Despite the rain…” or “In spite of the rain…”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: the difference between “despite” and “in spite of”.

truefalse.sentence: I've known him for ten years.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct. “know” is a state verb, so we don't use it in the continuous: “I've known”, not “I've been knowing”.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: can we use know in the continuous?

truefalse.sentence: She said me that she was busy.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. say something (to someone), tell someone. Correct: “She told me that…”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: say or tell?

truefalse.sentence: There are less cars in the village.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. With things you can count, use “fewer”. Correct: “There are fewer cars…”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: can you count cars?

truefalse.sentence: The number of tourists has doubled.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct. “The number of” is singular: has doubled. “A number of” is plural: have.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: the number of + has or have?

truefalse.sentence: I am living here since 2020.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. With “since” we use the present perfect: “I have lived / have been living here since 2020.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which tense goes with since?

truefalse.sentence: He made me to wait for an hour.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. make someone do (no “to”). Correct: “He made me wait for an hour.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: do you need “to” after “make”?

truefalse.sentence: It was such a boring film.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct. such a + adjective + noun. We don't say “so boring film”.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: so or such?

truefalse.sentence: I enjoy to read books.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. enjoy + -ing. Correct: “I enjoy reading books.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which form comes after enjoy?

truefalse.sentence: She has a lot of knowledges.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. You can't count “knowledge”. Correct: “She has a lot of knowledge.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: can knowledge take a plural -s?

truefalse.sentence: If I were you, I would apply.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct. When we give advice we say “If I were you”. We use “were” for every person.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: was or were when you give advice?

truefalse.sentence: The children is playing outside.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. “children” is plural. Correct: “The children are playing outside.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: is children singular?

truefalse.sentence: I prefer tea to coffee.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct. prefer A to B. We don't say “prefer tea than coffee”.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which preposition goes with “prefer”?

truefalse.sentence: He works as a engineer.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. Before a vowel sound we use “an”: an engineer.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: a or an?

truefalse.sentence: She is married to a doctor.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct. be married to someone. We don't say “married with”.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which preposition goes with “married”?

truefalse.sentence: I didn't use to like vegetables.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct. In the negative we write “didn't use to” (no d).
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: how do we write “used to” in the negative?

truefalse.sentence: Every students must bring an ID.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. every + singular noun. Correct: “Every student must bring an ID.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: is the noun after “every” singular?

truefalse.sentence: We arrived to the airport late.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. arrive at (a building, a place) / arrive in (a city). Correct: “We arrived at the airport late.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which preposition goes with “arrive”?

truefalse.sentence: Smoking is harmful to health.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct. An -ing form (gerund) can be the subject of a sentence.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: can a sentence start with an -ing form?

truefalse.sentence: I am boring in this lesson.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. For feelings we use -ed: “I am bored.” -ing describes the thing: “The lesson is boring.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: bored or boring?

truefalse.sentence: Hardly ever do I eat fast food.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct. When a sentence starts with “hardly ever”, the word order changes (inversion): do I eat. Band 8 grammar!
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: have you heard of inversion?

truefalse.sentence: Who did call you yesterday?
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. When we ask about the subject, we don't need “did”: “Who called you yesterday?”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: is the question about the subject?

truefalse.sentence: It's the best film I've ever seen.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct. Superlative + I've ever + past participle.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which tense goes with “the best … ever”?

truefalse.sentence: I need an information about the course.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. You can't count “information”: “some information” or “a piece of information”.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: can we put “an” before “information”?

truefalse.sentence: He stopped to smoke last year.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. If he quit smoking: “He stopped smoking.” “stopped to smoke” means he stopped what he was doing so that he could smoke.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: the difference between stop + -ing and stop + to.

truefalse.sentence: Neither my brother nor I am good at maths.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct. With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearest subject: I am.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which subject does the verb agree with?

truefalse.sentence: By 2030, the population will reach 40 million.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct. We use “will” for predictions, and it is very common in Task 1 graphs about the future.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: a sentence for a graph about the future.

truefalse.sentence: This is the city where I was born in.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. “where” already shows the place, so “in” is not needed. Correct: “…where I was born.”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: do we need “where” and “in” together?

truefalse.sentence: Mathematics are my favourite subject.
truefalse.explanation: ❌ Wrong. Mathematics, physics, economics are singular: “Mathematics is…”
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: school subjects that end in -s.

truefalse.sentence: I wish I had more free time.
truefalse.explanation: ✅ Correct. For a wish about now, use wish + past simple: I wish I had.
truefalse.caption: 💡 Hint: which tense comes after “wish”?

redflag.title: Writing Task 2 habits
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
red: Copying the question word for word
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 The examiner knows a memorised sentence at once, and those words are not counted.
🟢 A 5-minute check catches 2–3 mistakes. That can change your score by half a band.

redflag.title: Speaking habits
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
red: Staying silent when you don't understand
green: Fixing a mistake and going on
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 The examiner notices a memorised answer at once and changes the topic.
🟢 Asking to hear the question again is completely normal. You don't lose points for it.

redflag.title: Listening habits
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
red: Getting stuck on the last question
green: Reading the next questions in the pause
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 The audio plays only once. If you get stuck on one question, you miss the next 3–4 too.
🟢 If you miss the letter “s”, the answer is still marked wrong.

redflag.title: Reading habits
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
red: Reading the text from start to end
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 Reading has 40 questions in 60 minutes. There is no time to understand every word.
🟢 A 20-minute limit for each passage is the simplest way to manage your time.

redflag.title: Task 1 habits
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
green: Only the information from the graph
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 Task 1 does not ask for your opinion. A sentence like “I think this is good” lowers your Task Achievement score.
🟢 With no overview, it is hard to get more than 5.5.

redflag.title: Habits for learning words
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 Your brain quickly forgets a word with no context.
🟢 A word you learned in a pair like “make a decision” comes out naturally when you speak.

redflag.title: Mock test habits
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 A test with no checking just takes your time.
🟢 One test and 1 hour of checking helps more than 3 tests with no checking.

redflag.title: Exam day habits
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
red: Studying all night with no sleep
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 A tired brain loses focus fast in Listening and Reading.
🟢 Don't learn new things on the last night. Rest well.

redflag.title: Speaking Part 2 habits
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 The examiner listens for 2 minutes. If you stop early, your Fluency score goes down.
🟢 The 4 points on the card are a ready plan: speak for 30 seconds on each and the time fills up.

redflag.title: Pronunciation habits
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
red: Saying words one by one like a robot
Putting the stress in the wrong place
green: Checking the stress in a dictionary
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 Speaking fast is not fluency. Speech that is hard to understand lowers your Pronunciation score.
🟢 Small pauses between groups of words make your speech natural.

redflag.title: Grammar habits
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 With only simple sentences, your Grammatical Range score stays at 6 or lower.
🟢 A small mistake in a complex sentence gets a better mark than a simple sentence with no mistakes.

redflag.title: Your phone and studying
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
red: Keeping your phone next to you
Studying for 3 hours with no break
green: Putting your phone in another room
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 After each notification you need about 20 minutes to get your focus back.
🟢 The 25+5 method (Pomodoro) helps you study for a long time and not get tired.

redflag.title: Online materials
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
red: A new course or channel every day
green: Practising at once what you watched
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 Many sources = a lot of information, but few results.
🟢 Practice gives you points, not watching videos. Practise for 15 minutes after each lesson.

redflag.title: Writing Task 1 mistakes
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 With no overview, your Task Achievement stays at 5 or lower.
🟢 Grouping the trends saves words and makes your analysis stronger.

redflag.title: Vocabulary habits
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
red: Using a hard word in the wrong place
Using one word again and again
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 A “hard” word used in the wrong way lowers your score more than a simple word.
🟢 A word learned with its collocation (make a decision) sounds natural.

redflag.title: Speaking Part 3 habits
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
green: Adding a reason and a result
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 In Part 3 the examiner marks how you think. “I don't know” is not an answer.
🟢 Start with “I'd imagine…” or “Perhaps…” and develop your idea.

redflag.title: Listening Section 4 habits
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
green: Skipping it and moving to the next one
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 Section 4 has no break. If you freeze on one answer, you lose the next 3 too.
🟢 Write a guess for a missed answer at the end. Don't leave it empty.

redflag.title: Essay planning habits
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
red: Starting to write with no plan
Answering only one part of the question
Changing your opinion at the end
green: Marking every part of the question
Keeping your position from start to end
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 If you answer only one part of a two-part question, your Task Response stays at 5 or lower.
🟢 5 minutes of planning makes your writing time shorter.

redflag.title: Different grammar structures
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 Only simple sentences keep your Grammatical Range at 5–5.5.
🟢 Adding one complex sentence to each answer makes enough difference.

redflag.title: Reading True/False/Not Given
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
red: Using what you know from life
Saying True because one word matches
Mixing up Not Given and False
green: Comparing the meaning of the whole sentence
Opposite in the text = False, not there = Not Given
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 A fact that is true in life but not in the text is still Not Given.
🟢 For False, the text must clearly say the opposite.

redflag.title: Practice habits
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
green: More time for your weakest part
Writing every mistake in a notebook
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 Practising your strong part feels good, but your weak part decides your overall score.
🟢 In one month, a mistake notebook shows you the problems you repeat the most.

redflag.title: Feeling nervous in Speaking
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
green: Fixing the mistake and going on
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 Speaking fast gives you more pronunciation mistakes, and the examiner can't understand you.
🟢 Correcting yourself is really a good sign.

redflag.title: Sleep and the exam
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
red: Studying all night before the exam
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 No sleep means less focus, and you feel it at once in Listening and Reading.
🟢 The exam takes about 3 hours, so use your energy wisely.

redflag.title: The Task 2 introduction
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
red: Hiding your opinion until the conclusion
green: Giving your position in the introduction
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 A long introduction steals time from your main ideas.
🟢 The examiner should see your opinion in the first paragraph.

redflag.title: English around you
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
red: Not speaking because you fear mistakes
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 2 hours of lessons a week is not enough to learn a language.
🟢 Small daily habits make a big difference in one month.

redflag.title: Spelling habits
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
green: A list of words you spell wrong
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 In Listening, a spelling mistake makes the whole answer wrong.
🟢 There is no autocorrect in the exam, so you need to practise by hand.

redflag.title: Matching headings habits
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
red: Choosing a heading about an example
green: Reading the first and last sentences
Crossing out the headings you used
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 If a heading repeats a word from the text, it is often a trap.
🟢 The main idea of a paragraph is usually in the first or last sentence.

redflag.title: Waiting for your result
redflag.subtitle: Which ones do you have? Be honest
red: Stopping your studies until the result comes
No plan to retake only one part
Blaming other people for your mistakes
green: Practising your weak part while you wait
redflag.caption:
Why does this matter?
🚩 A 2-week break makes you forget what you learned.
🟢 In computer-delivered IELTS you can retake only one part.

redflag.title: Studying with AI and ChatGPT

band.title: One question, two answers
subtitle: Swipe: first Band 5, then Band 8
Can you see the difference?
band.question: Describe your hometown.
band.band5: My hometown is Samarkand. It is very beautiful. There are many old buildings. I like it very much.
band.band8: I'm from Samarkand, a city steeped in history. It's renowned for its breathtaking architecture, especially the Registan.
band.caption: 📚 What the Band 8 words mean: ▫️ steeped in history = having a lot of history ▫️ renowned for = famous for ▫️ breathtaking = very beautiful and surprising 💡 The Band 5 answer repeats basic words. The Band 8 answer uses exact, strong phrases.

band.caption: 📚 What the Band 8 words mean: ▫️ switched to = changed to ▫️ streaming platforms = websites and apps for watching films online 💡 The Band 5 answer repeats basic words. The Band 8 answer uses exact, strong phrases.

pov.question: Do you like pets?
pov.better: Yes, I'm a huge animal lover. I've had a cat for five years and she's the best company after a long day.
vocab: a person who loves animals very much
the nicest one to spend time with
pov.lesson: A one-word answer lowers your Fluency score. Formula: answer + reason + example.

pov.question: What do you do?
pov.better: I'm a second-year student at university, majoring in economics. It's demanding, but I really enjoy it.
vocab: studying as your main subject at university
hard, needing a lot of effort
pov.lesson: Not “I'm student” but “I'm a student”. Leaving out the article is one of the most common mistakes.

pov.question: Do you like your hometown?
pov.bad: Yes, I like. Because it is beautiful.
pov.better: Absolutely. It's steeped in history, and I love wandering around the old town in the evenings.
vocab: walking around slowly with no plan
pov.lesson: After “I like” you need an object: I like it. And “Because” can't start a sentence that stands alone.

pov.question: You have one minute to prepare. Please start.
pov.better: I'd like to talk about… What I remember most is… Looking back, I think…
vocab: when I think about the past now
pov.lesson: In Part 2 you must speak for 2 minutes. Ready “bridge” phrases make your talk longer in a natural way.

pov.question: Why do young people use social media so much?
pov.better: That's an interesting question. I suppose it keeps them connected with friends, and it's also a huge source of entertainment.
vocab: something that people enjoy in their free time
pov.lesson: In Part 3, don't say “I don't know”. Say a thinking phrase and make a guess.

pov.question: Do you enjoy cooking?
pov.better: Not really, to be honest. I'm hopeless in the kitchen, so I usually leave it to my mum.
vocab: to let another person do it
pov.lesson: “No” can be an answer too, just add a reason. A negative answer can get a good score.

pov.question: What's the weather like in your country?
pov.better: It varies a lot. Summers are scorching, often over 40 degrees, while winters can be quite chilly.
pov.lesson: Use an exact adjective in place of “very hot”. Comparing with “while” makes your answer richer.

pov.question: Do you read books?
pov.better: I do, but mostly on my phone. I've recently got into self-help books, like Atomic Habits.
pov.lesson: Don't repeat the words of the question: say “I do” and add new information.

pov.question: Where are you from?
pov.better: I'm from Tashkent, the capital of Uzbekistan. It's a lively city with a mix of old and modern architecture.
pov.lesson: This is the very first question of Part 1. Describe your city in 2 sentences, not in one word.

pov.question: Do you like to travel?
pov.bad: Yes, I like travel very much.
pov.better: Definitely! I try to go somewhere new every summer. Last year I explored the mountains near Chimgan.
vocab: to travel around a place to learn about it
to visit a place for the first time
pov.lesson: Not “like travel” but “like travelling” or “like to travel”. And add one clear example.

pov.question: Do you think people read less nowadays?
pov.better: To some extent, yes. Fewer people read printed books, but I'd argue we read more than ever, just in shorter forms online.
pov.lesson: In Part 3, show two sides: “yes, but…”. This gives you a higher score.

pov.question: Thank you, that's the end of the test.
pov.better: Thank you. Have a nice day!
vocab: a friendly way to say goodbye
It was nice talking to you
a polite thing to say at the end of a conversation
pov.lesson: The examiner is not your teacher, so don't call them “teacher”. A simple “Thank you” is enough.

pov.question: What did you do last weekend?
pov.better: I visited my grandparents in the countryside. We had a big family lunch, which was lovely.
pov.lesson: When the question is about the past, use the Past Simple: went, visited, had.

pov.question: Do you like music?
pov.better: Absolutely, I'm really into pop and lo-fi. I usually put some on while I'm studying because it helps me focus.
pov.lesson: After “I like”, say what you like. Formula: answer + what + when.

pov.question: Do you work or study?
pov.better: I'm currently a second-year student at a university in Tashkent, majoring in economics.
pov.lesson: Don't give a one-word answer. Answer with a full sentence.

pov.question: Describe a gift you received.
pov.bad: My friend gave me a watch. It was good.
pov.better: I'd like to talk about a watch my best friend gave me on my 18th birthday. What made it special was that she'd engraved my name on the back.
vocab: the thing that made it different and important
pov.lesson: In Part 2, add details with phrases like “what made it special”.

pov.question: Is it better to live in a city or the countryside?
pov.better: It depends on your stage of life. For young people, cities offer more opportunities, whereas the countryside suits families looking for peace.
pov.lesson: In Part 3, compare the two sides, then give your opinion.

pov.question: Do you like sports?
pov.better: Not really, to be honest. I've never been a sporty person, but I do go for long walks to clear my head.
vocab: I've never been a sporty person
I have never liked doing sport
to make my mind calm and fresh
pov.lesson: You can say “No”, but then give a reason and say what you do in its place.

pov.question: What do you do in your free time?
pov.better: When I have some spare time, I mostly watch YouTube videos about science or travel. It's a great way to unwind.
vocab: to relax after work or study
pov.lesson: Name the activity clearly and add why you like it.

pov.question: Do you prefer mornings or evenings?
pov.better: I'm definitely a night owl. My brain only really wakes up after sunset, so I do my best work in the evenings.
vocab: a person who is active late at night
to work in the best way I can
pov.lesson: An idiom used in a natural way raises your Lexical Resource score.

pov.question: Can you repeat the question, please?
pov.better: Sorry, could you repeat the question, please?
vocab: a polite word before you ask
pov.lesson: If you don't understand the question, ask politely. You don't lose points for it.

pov.question: Should the government spend more on public transport?
pov.better: I'd say so, yes. Better public transport would ease congestion and cut pollution, which benefits everyone, not just commuters.
pov.lesson: Opinion + 2 reasons + who it helps. The Part 3 formula.

pov.question: Describe a time you helped someone.
pov.bad: I helped my neighbour. It was nice.
pov.better: I'm going to describe a time I helped my elderly neighbour move house. It took a whole day, but seeing how grateful she was made it worth it.
vocab: to go to live in a new home
it was good enough for the hard work
pov.lesson: In Part 2, finish with a feeling: how you felt.

pov.question: Do you use public transport?
pov.better: Yes, quite often. I take the metro to university because it's fast and much cheaper than a taxi.
pov.lesson: Make “Sometimes” longer: when and why.

pov.question: Do you like shopping?
pov.better: Not particularly. I find crowded malls exhausting, so I tend to shop online instead.
pov.lesson: Don't repeat the words of the question. Paraphrase them.

pov.question: How has your city changed in recent years?
pov.better: It's changed beyond recognition. Lots of modern high-rises have gone up, and the metro has been extended to the suburbs.
vocab: so much that you can't recognise it
pov.lesson: Use the present perfect to talk about changes.

pov.question: What's your favourite season?
pov.better: I'd have to say spring. The weather's mild, everything's in bloom, and it's perfect for long walks.
vocab: a natural way to start your answer
pov.lesson: “I'd have to say” sounds very natural at the start of an answer.

pov.question: Do you think robots will replace teachers?
pov.better: I doubt it. While AI can deliver information, it can't replace the emotional support and motivation a good teacher provides.
vocab: I don't think it will happen
pov.lesson: Accept the other side with “While…”, then give your own opinion.

pov.question: Do you have a lot of friends?
pov.better: I wouldn't say a lot, but I have a small circle of close friends I can always count on.
vocab: to trust someone to help you
pov.lesson: Quality matters more than quantity: give clear details.

pov.question: Tell me about your hometown.
pov.better: I'm from Bukhara, which is one of the oldest cities in Central Asia. It's famous for its well-preserved mosques and madrasas.
vocab: older than almost all the others
pov.lesson: After the name of the city, add an interesting fact with “which…”.

pov.question: Do you like getting up early?
pov.better: Honestly, not at all. I'm not a morning person, so I need at least two cups of tea to function properly.
vocab: a person who does not feel good early in the morning
to work in the normal way
pov.lesson: After “I don't like” you need an object. It is even better to answer with a full sentence.
